passage:
Mentor's note, Friday. Arohi stopped by the department office to say she had won the summer research place. She was still smiling, but by the end of the visit her voice had dropped. She told me she'd rushed to tell her partner Kamal first, and he had answered with a joke: "They must have run out of applicants." Then he changed the subject to his own exam.

She laughed it off in front of me, but her hands kept smoothing the corner of her folder. She admitted she had stopped mentioning things to him in case he sulked.

I said only that coldness at good news is worth noticing, and worth mentioning to him kindly. She said she would try, and that she had already told her hostel friends, who screamed with joy. She left looking lighter.

qa.q: What news did Arohi bring to the department office?
qa.a: She told the mentor she had won the summer research place.

qa.q: What might Arohi be feeling as she laughs off the joke while smoothing the corner of her folder?
qa.a: Hurt and unsure: her voice dropped by the end of the visit, and she had already stopped mentioning things to Kamal in case he sulked.

qa.q: What could Arohi do about Kamal's reaction to her news?
qa.a: Tell Kamal kindly how his joke landed, and keep sharing her wins with the friends who cheer for her instead of hiding them.

qa.q: What might Kamal be feeling when he answers her news with a joke and turns to his own exam?
qa.a: Kamal might feel smaller or worried about his own progress, so he may be deflecting instead of sharing her happiness.

grounding: Shows good news met with a coldness and a joke, the affected person noticing and still sharing wins with people who cheer.

passage: Karthik, you've stopped telling your girlfriend about your marks, haven't you? I saw your face at lunch. Let your Pema Ani tell you something that happened to me. At twenty-one, in Darjeeling, I won a scholarship to study nursing in Delhi. I ran to tell Norbu, the boy I was seeing. He said, 'Delhi? Good, now you'll think you're too big for us,' laughed, and changed the subject. Every good thing after that, he had a joke ready. So I started hiding things. I didn't tell him when I topped the first term. I felt like I was shrinking myself to keep him comfortable. Then my sister said, 'Pema, why are you whispering your own news?' So I sat Norbu down and said, kindly, 'When you joke about my wins, it hurts. I want you to be happy for me.' He tried for a while. It didn't last, and we parted. But I never whispered my good news again.

qa.q: What did Norbu say when Pema told him about the scholarship?
qa.a: 'Delhi? Good, now you'll think you're too big for us.'

qa.q: How did Pema feel hiding her first-term result?
qa.a: She felt small, as if shrinking herself to keep Norbu comfortable.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Pema's story?
qa.a: Her sister asking why she whispered her own news, which led Pema to talk kindly but honestly with Norbu.

qa.q: How might Norbu have felt about Pema's scholarship?
qa.a: Probably envious and insecure, afraid she would outgrow him, which came out as jokes.

grounding: An elder's story of good news met with cold jokes, noticing it, talking kindly, and refusing to hide success to protect a partner's ego.

passage: Gurleen got the offer letter at noon: a design job at a studio she'd dreamed about since first year. By one o'clock she had told Chetan, who had been rejected by three firms that month. 'Nice,' he texted. Just that. At his cousin's engagement party that evening, loud with dhol and relatives, someone congratulated her, and Chetan said, 'Yeah, she's the famous one now. I just carry her bags.' People laughed. Gurleen's cheeks burned. She almost played it down: 'It's only a junior role.' She stopped herself. Outside, by the parked cars, she said quietly, 'Chetan, that joke hurt. I know this month's been awful for you, and I'm sorry. But I'm not going to hide good news to make things easier.' He looked at his shoes. 'I'm jealous. I hate that I'm jealous.' 'Then tell me that, not the room.' Later that night she called her best friend, who screamed with joy down the phone. Gurleen let herself feel it fully.

qa.q: What did Chetan say at the engagement party?
qa.a: 'Yeah, she's the famous one now. I just carry her bags.'

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when people laughed at the joke?
qa.a: Her cheeks burned with hurt and embarrassment.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do instead of playing down her news?
qa.a: She told Chetan kindly that the joke hurt, refused to hide her success, and celebrated with a friend who cheered.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling underneath the joke?
qa.a: Jealousy, after a month of rejections, which he admits and hates feeling.

grounding: Shows a young woman whose good news is met with a cold joke, talking kindly with her partner and celebrating with someone who cheers instead of hiding it.
